T4.2-9.why: An evidence pack is what an auditor opens to see that a control works. Claiming a file that does not exist is worse than recording a gap.
T4.2-9.h1: For every sub-task of LI-A.5.7, ask: do I already hold this item, can I prepare it from the facts, or does nothing at the office show it yet?
T4.2-9.h3: Reasoning: reuse a deliverable you already made when it truly holds the item, since one record should not be written twice. Prepare a new file only from facts the dataset gives. Where the dataset says the check, list or rating was never done, choose None and write the gap and the next action, because inventing an item makes the record false. Check the file name matches your 02_Working naming.

T5.1-1.why: The plan turns a rated risk into work with an owner and a date. Knowing a finished row first stops half-filled plans.
T5.1-1.h1: Read the two LearnTech rows and list what each column holds, then read the facts on your own three rows.
T5.1-1.h3: Reasoning: a finished row has an option, the controls that carry it out, Annex A IDs, a named owner, a date, the residual rating and the approver. Note which facts on your rows will decide the option, such as how many ways in, whether something can be switched off, and how the residual score compares with the appetite.

T5.1-2.why: Treatment is where the organisation chooses what to do about a risk. A consistent rule keeps the choice from depending on who asks.
T5.1-2.h1: Apply rule L12's four questions in order to each row, comparing its residual score with the appetite.
T5.1-2.h3: Reasoning: do not choose the option you like. Ask the questions in order and stop at the first that applies. The facts that settle each are in the row: whether the asset is still needed, whether the residual score is within the appetite, and whether a control can reduce it. Different rows can end up with different options.

T5.1-3.why: A control that acts on nothing wastes money, and a necessary control that is left out leaves the risk standing.
T5.1-3.h1: For each proposed control, ask whether it acts on the cause, the event or the consequence in the risk statement. Then find its Annex A match.
T5.1-3.h3: Reasoning: needed means the control changes this risk, not that it is a good idea in general. Read the risk statement and mark its cause, its event and its consequence; a proposed control that touches none of the three belongs to some other risk, however sensible it is. For each needed control, read the Annex A titles and pick the one whose purpose matches, not just one that shares a word. The comparison is a check that nothing necessary was left out (Clause 6.1.3 c).

T5.1-4.why: Treating Annex A as the only source would stop you using a control that works. Ignoring it would let necessary controls go missing.
T5.1-4.h1: Re-read Clause 6.1.3 b) and c): what are the controls chosen from, and what is Annex A used for?
T5.1-4.h3: Reasoning: read the Clause 6.1.3 entry, items b) and c). Note two things: where it says controls may be chosen from, and what job it gives Annex A. Then test each choice: does the clause restrict you to one list, and does it mention anyone's prior agreement?

T5.1-5.why: The people who live with the residual risk should be the ones who agree to carry it.
T5.1-5.h1: Recall Clause 6.1.3 f): who approves the plan and who accepts the risks that remain.
T5.1-5.h3: Reasoning: acceptance belongs with the person who has the authority and accountability for the risk, which you identified when you set up risk ownership. People who run the system or check it do not own the risks and cannot accept them on the organisation's behalf.

T5.1-6.why: A treatment with no date never happens, and an acceptance with no expiry becomes permanent without anyone deciding it.
T5.1-6.h1: Look up days by rating in R08, count them from the plan's date, then fill the acceptance columns for the one risk you keep.
T5.1-6.h3: Reasoning: the number of days depends on the rating (R08, SITL-ERM-001 Section 7), and counting starts at the plan's date stated in the step. A risk you treat needs only its due date. For the risk you retain, SITL-POL-002 Section 6.2 sets each column: the reason is given against the appetite, the expiry and the re-assessment date are each counted at the interval that section sets for the residual rating, and the approver is the authority R36 names for that score.

T5.1-7.why: A saved file with a hash and a UTC time is proof of what you handed in and when. A reviewer or auditor trusts a record they can check, not a file name.
T5.1-7.h1: Name LI-RTP by the convention shown on the step, save, then read the receipt before you mark the step complete.
T5.1-7.h3: The hash proves the file has not changed since you saved it, and the UTC time fixes when, in a clock nobody can argue about. If you mark the step complete before the receipt shows, you have nothing to point to if the hand-in is questioned. A wrong name also breaks later steps that look the file up by its name.

T5.2-1.why: The SoA is the document an auditor opens first. Knowing how a finished row reads, and where the carried-over cells came from, lets you complete the other rows consistently.
T5.2-1.h1: Read the LearnTech worked row across all its columns, then find where your own tracker's entries appear.
T5.2-1.h3: The first row is a worked example for another company, so it shows the shape of a good row: the source named, the inclusion justification written, the status and evidence reference filled. Compare it with a row for a control you already sprinted in your CIT files; those Implemented? and Evidence ref cells were carried over, not typed. Rule L07 says the not-yet-sprinted controls must say when they are planned.

T5.2-10.why: An objective nobody can measure cannot be reported in the management review, so Clause 6.2 asks for objectives you can check.
T5.2-10.h1: A measurable objective says what is counted, a target and a date. Check each choice against all three.
T5.2-10.h3: Clause 6.2 b says objectives must be measurable. The Quick Reference spells that out as a thing that is counted, a target to reach and a date. Test each line by asking what you would count, what number would count as success, and by when. A line that names an intention or an activity without a number cannot be reported against.

T5.2-11.why: Objectives with no owner, action or date never get done. Clause 6.2 asks for what will be done, who is responsible, what resources and when.
T5.2-11.h1: Match each objective to one of the four gaps in its row, then ask who is Responsible for that area in the Charter RACI.
T5.2-11.h3: Start from the four gap rows in the sheet and write one objective for each; each must follow the measurable rule L14: a counted thing, a target and a date, and agree with SITL-POL-001. For the person, read Section 16 of the Charter, the RACI, for the R role of that area. For the plan, say what will be done, with what, and when it will be finished. Keep each objective to one measure so it can be reported on its own.

T5.2-12.why: Auditors ask when a record was created and that it has not changed since. The hash and UTC time in the receipt are that proof.
T5.2-12.h1: Name LI-SOA and LI-OBJ by the convention, save, and read the receipt before marking complete.
T5.2-12.h3: The naming convention is shown in the step text; follow its order of parts exactly and keep each file name unique to its content. After you click Save to 02_Working the receipt shows a hash and a UTC time. If either is missing, the save did not complete, so save again. Only when you can see both should you click Mark step complete.

T5.2-2.why: Clause 6.1.3 d asks you to justify every Annex A decision. A reason that names a real source can be defended in the audit; a bare yes cannot.
T5.2-2.h1: For each control read its SOA-93 fact and ask what, if anything, in it calls for the control.
T5.2-2.h3: Rule L06 says a control applies when something in the file calls for it, and the source you record is the first of those that fits, in that order. Read each control's fact at Manila: it names what calls for it, such as a regulation, an agreement, a treated risk or a Group rule. Exclude only when the office genuinely does nothing the control governs. Work through the rows in order and keep your reading of the source order the same every time.

T5.2-3.why: Excluding a control without a recorded reason fails Clause 6.1.3 d. The SoA must list all 93 controls and say why any is left out.
T5.2-3.h1: Think about what the SoA must show for every Annex A control, even one the office does not use.
T5.2-3.h3: Rule L06 allows exclusion only when the office does nothing the control governs, and it requires the justification to be recorded. The row never leaves the SoA, because the standard asks you to justify excluding a control rather than silently drop it. Ask which choice records the fact about Manila, gives its reason, and still says when to look again if the facts change.

T5.2-4.why: The SoA is a named required output, and an auditor tests it against the clause. Knowing its four elements stops you leaving one out of the real document.
T5.2-4.h1: Recall Clause 6.1.3 d and ask which list matches what the clause actually requires the SoA to contain.
T5.2-4.h3: Open the Quick Reference entry for Clause 6.1.3 d. It lists what the SoA holds in four parts. Write the four down, then compare each choice with them, part by part. Ask also where the other choices' items would normally be kept: a project plan and a risk register are records too, but different ones.

T5.2-5.why: The SoA and the plan for treating risks describe the same decisions from two sides. If they disagree, the auditor cannot tell which one is true.
T5.2-5.h1: Ask which output the controls in the SoA come from, and what Clause 6.1.3 says about their relationship.
T5.2-5.h3: Clause 6.1.3 b to e runs in sequence: risk treatment determines which controls are necessary, the SoA records them, and a treatment plan is then formulated from them. So the SoA has to agree with the output that determined the controls. Check each choice against that chain and ask which of them would be changed if a control were added or dropped.

T5.2-6.why: The tracker is the single place the programme records where each control stands, so you open it before deciding anything, and owners come from roles not names.
T5.2-6.h1: Find the worked row and the LI page for A.5.8; read them before you touch your own rows.
T5.2-6.h3: The tracker opens with columns A to G filtered to this sprint. Read the worked row to see how a finished row looks, then open the LI page for A.5.8 and note its owner role and what it requires. The Quick Reference and the SOA-93 observation for it are your sources in the next steps. The task here is to read and locate; you will decide status and maturity in the next steps.

T5.2-7.why: A control's status tells management what is really in place. Overstating it hides work still owed, and the auditor finds it later.
T5.2-7.h1: Take A.5.8 one requirement at a time and ask whether the SOA-93 observation shows it is met.
T5.2-7.h3: Open the LI task page for A.5.8 and read its 'What it requires' list. Then read the SOA-93 observation for the same control. For each requirement, ask whether the observation shows it exists today; a plan, an intention or a draft does not count. If every requirement is shown, say so; if only some are, or none, say that. A requirement met in one place but missing in another is only partly met. Check the note on the sheet that defines the three statuses before you choose.

T5.2-8.why: Maturity shows how far a control can be trusted to keep working. An auditor asks for records and review, so rating it high without them fails in the audit room.
T5.2-8.h1: Ask the Maturity Model questions in order for A.5.8 and stop at the first one the SOA-93 observation cannot answer yes to.
T5.2-8.h3: Open Ref-Maturity Model under Learn, Reference pages. The questions are ordered: is it documented and approved, with records; is it the Group's standard way, used in every office and reviewed; is it measured. Take the SOA-93 observation for A.5.8 and answer each in turn. The first question that gets a no sets the level, whatever is true further down. A good practice only in Manila, or an approved document nobody has reviewed, stops the climb early.

T5.2-9.why: Evidence is what lets you prove a control to an auditor. A pack with the right file against each sub-task shows you can, and a gap listed honestly is better than a file that does not fit.
T5.2-9.h1: For each sub-task, check whether you already made a file for it, then whether the SOA-93 observation holds the records to prepare one.
T5.2-9.h3: Work down the sub-tasks in the A.5.8 LI page. For each, follow the order on the sheet: first a file you made in an earlier task, then a new item prepared from what the SOA-93 observation says exists, and only then None with the gap recorded. Name the file as it sits in 02_Working. Do not put a file against a sub-task it does not evidence just to fill the cell; a gap you record can be fixed, one you hide cannot.

T6.1-1.why: Clause 7.2 starts with what each role needs to be competent in. You must see that first, because you cannot judge a person against a need you have not read.
T6.1-1.h1: Read the two worked rows and see what HR holds and what action was chosen, then read your own rows' needs.
T6.1-1.h3: Each of the ten role holders has the competence their role needs, taken from what the role runs in your LI-RACI from T3.2. The worked rows show how HR records and the Action column fit together. Note that one of your roles needs competence for the management review, which comes from your RACI, not from the person's job title.

T6.1-10.why: Auditors ask when a record was created and that it has not changed since. The hash and UTC time in the receipt are that proof.
T6.1-10.h1: Name LI-COMM and AWR-PLAN by the convention, save, and read the receipt before marking complete.
T6.1-10.h3: The naming convention is shown in the step text; follow its order of parts exactly and keep each file name unique to its content. After you click Save to 02_Working the receipt shows a hash and a UTC time. If either is missing, the save did not complete, so save again. Only when you can see both should you click Mark step complete.

T6.1-2.why: Clause 7.2 requires you to keep evidence of competence. A skilled person with no record is still a gap an auditor will write up.
T6.1-2.h1: Compare three things on each row: what the role needs, the person's CV, and the HR records on file.
T6.1-2.h3: Apply Clause 7.2 a to d and SITL-POL-020 section 3.1. Read the competence the role needs, then what the CV shows, then what HR actually holds. A person can have the skill and still lack a record, which is a different finding from lacking the skill, and the action differs: train in one case, document in the other. The two worked rows show the pattern. Choose an action for every row that is not simply in good order.

T6.1-3.why: What you keep is what you can show an auditor. Clause 7.2 names the one thing you must hold to prove competence.
T6.1-3.h1: Recall Clause 7.2 d and ask what kind of thing it says to keep as evidence.
T6.1-3.h3: Read Clause 7.2 d in the Quick Reference and note what it says to keep, and as evidence of what. Ask of each choice whether it is evidence of someone's ability to do the job, whether it is proportionate to that purpose, and whether it is something the clause actually names.

T6.1-4.why: Awareness is a requirement on everyone working under the organisation's control, not only the security team, and Clause 7.3 lists exactly three things.
T6.1-4.h1: Clause 7.3 a to c lists three items. Find the choice that matches them.
T6.1-4.h3: Read Clause 7.3 in the Quick Reference and write down its three items, a to c. All three are about the management system and the person's own part in it. Check each choice against those three, and ask whether business performance or contracts appear anywhere in the clause.

T6.1-5.why: A message that nobody sends, or sends to the wrong people, leaves the ISMS unknown. Clause 7.4 asks what, when, with whom and how.
T6.1-5.h1: For each of the five messages find its row in the Group communication plan, then fill in when, who and how.
T6.1-5.h3: Clause 7.4 asks you to decide what to communicate, when, with whom and how. Use the Group ISMS communication plan row for each kind of message. For the incident lesson, check the condition on the row and the severity named in the message text before you decide who receives it. Keep the audience and the channel consistent with the row, not invented.

T6.1-6.why: The tracker is the single place the programme records where each control stands, so you open it before deciding anything, and owners come from roles not names.
T6.1-6.h1: Find the worked row and the LI page for A.6.3; read them before you touch your own rows.
T6.1-6.h3: The tracker opens with columns A to G filtered to this sprint. Read the worked row to see how a finished row looks, then open the LI page for A.6.3 and note its owner role and what it requires. Look at columns F and G and the Observed column. The task here is to read and locate; you will decide status and maturity in the next steps.

T6.1-7.why: A control's status tells management what is really in place. Overstating it hides work still owed, and the auditor finds it later.
T6.1-7.h1: Take A.6.3 one requirement at a time and ask whether the SPR-04 observation shows it is met.
T6.1-7.h3: Open the LI task page for A.6.3 and read its 'What it requires' list. Then read the SPR-04 observation for the same control. For each requirement, ask whether the observation shows it exists today; a plan, an intention or a draft does not count. If every requirement is shown, say so; if only some are, or none, say that. A requirement met in one place but missing in another is only partly met. Check the note on the sheet that defines the three statuses before you choose.

T6.1-8.why: Maturity shows how far a control can be trusted to keep working. An auditor asks for records and review, so rating it high without them fails in the audit room.
T6.1-8.h1: Ask the Maturity Model questions in order for A.6.3 and stop at the first one the SPR-04 observation cannot answer yes to.
T6.1-8.h3: Open Ref-Maturity Model under Learn, Reference pages. The questions are ordered: is it documented and approved, with records; is it the Group's standard way, used in every office and reviewed; is it measured. Take the SPR-04 observation for A.6.3 and answer each in turn. The first question that gets a no sets the level, whatever is true further down. A good practice only in Manila, or an approved document nobody has reviewed, stops the climb early.

T6.1-9.why: Evidence is what lets you prove a control to an auditor. A pack with the right file against each sub-task shows you can, and a gap listed honestly is better than a file that does not fit.
T6.1-9.h1: For each sub-task, check whether you already made a file for it, then whether SPR-04 holds the records to prepare one.
T6.1-9.h3: Work down the sub-tasks in the A.6.3 LI page. For each, follow the order on the sheet: first a file you hand in yourself, from an earlier task or this one, then a new item prepared from what SPR-04 says exists, and only then None with the gap recorded. Name the file as it sits in 02_Working. Do not put a file against a sub-task it does not evidence just to fill the cell; a gap you record can be fixed, one you hide cannot.

T6.2-1.why: Clause 7.5 treats a document you maintain differently from a record you retain, and the audit tests each differently, so getting the kind right decides what you must keep current.
T6.2-1.h1: Read the clause wording for each item and ask whether it asks for the thing itself or for evidence that something happened.
T6.2-1.h3: The Clause 7.5.1 rule in the step note: where the clause asks for the thing itself, it is a document you maintain; where it asks you to retain, or to have it available as evidence, it is a record. Read the 'What the clause asks for' column for each of the ten items and apply that test. Do not decide from what Manila happens to hold, which is the next column.

Use roles from those sections, not names you invent.

T6.2-7.h1: For each control take sub-task 01 of its LI page for column F, then pick the next step up from the level you gave it for G.
T6.2-7.h3: Column F takes the file for sub-task 01 of the other five controls: reuse one of your own files if it fits, otherwise a new item prepared from SPR-05. T6.2-8.why: Starting before screening protects nobody and exposes the company. A.6.1 expects screening to be proportionate and any exception to be managed.
T6.2-8.h1: Ask what A.6.1 requires before someone joins, and what should happen when that was not done.
T6.2-8.h3: Use the LI-A.6.1 requirements and sub-task 03 plus the SPR-05 observation. Two questions settle it. When does the control place screening relative to the start date, and does it scale with the role's risk? And when a check was missed, what does the control expect to be written down, and what about the person's access in the meantime? Check each choice for both parts.

T6.2-9.why: Auditors ask when a record was created and that it has not changed since. The hash and UTC time in the receipt are that proof.
T6.2-9.h1: Name LI-DOC and CIT-S5 by the convention, save, and read the receipt before marking complete.
T6.2-9.h3: The naming convention is shown in the step text; follow its order of parts exactly and keep each file name unique to its content. After you click Save to 02_Working the receipt shows a hash and a UTC time. If either is missing, the save did not complete, so save again. Only when you can see both should you click Mark step complete.

T7.1-1.h3: On each line read the role's duties, who the role reports to, the system and its asset owner, and the access held today. Choose the level from the list on the sheet that the duties need (SITL-POL-006 Section 3.1), not the level the role holds now; where the two differ, the line is a finding. For the approver, read Section 6.1 step 2: it names two approvals in order, and both people are on the line itself.

T7.1-7.why: Leavers who keep access are a classic breach route. Recording it as an exception with a root cause, not a shrug, is what the control expects.
T7.1-7.h1: Compare the three days with the time the policy sets, then decide what must happen now and what you must record.
T7.1-7.h3: SITL-POL-006 section 3.1 and 6.3 set the time within which a leaver's access must go, and say any use after termination is an incident. Three days is beyond that, so ask whether this is acceptable or a departure, what you do today about the live account, and what you check to learn whether it was used. A good record names the departure, the action and the cause.

T7.1-8.why: Shared accounts break accountability, because nobody can say who did what. A.5.16 is about identities that can be traced.
T7.1-8.h1: Ask what conditions the control sets on a shared identity, and what it still wants to be able to show afterwards.
T7.1-8.h3: Read the LI-A.5.16 requirement on shared identities and the SPR-06 account observation. Note each condition the requirement sets and what it says about tracing an action to a person. Then test each choice: does it state those conditions, or only an absolute, for or against?

T7.2-1.why: Tier decides how hard you look at a supplier. Under-tiering a supplier that holds sensitive data leaves your biggest risk with your lightest checks.
T7.2-1.h1: Read each supplier's intake form and use the term definitions in the policy, not your own sense of 'big' or 'small'.
T7.2-1.h3: Rule R35 uses terms defined in SITL-POL-013 section 3.1, with a table that says to read them on the intake form. For each supplier, mark which terms its intake lines meet, such as the data it holds or the access it has, and apply the rule to get the tier. Special-category data raises the tier. Do not tier by the contract value or by how well you know the vendor.

T7.2-2.h3: On VEN-CL, use the 'Required from tier' and 'The contract must say' columns, then compare with 'What the contract says' and the hosting location. Rule R27 and POL-013 section 6.3 define the three outcomes for a clause. A clause that is there but weaker than required is not the same as one that is absent. Decide per clause, not per supplier.

T7.2-8.why: In the cloud, responsibility is split. If you assume the provider does everything you miss your own share, and that is where cloud breaches happen.
T7.2-8.h1: Look at the SaaS row of the cloud reference and ask what the provider secures and what stays with the customer.
T7.2-8.h3: Ref-Cloud has a row for each service model, and rule L19 gives the model for this tool. Read that model's row: it says what the provider secures and what remains with the customer. Find application patching in one of the two lists. Then fill the matrix in LI-CLD, taking the model from the intake form and marking each duty to the right party.

T7.2-9.why: A supplier holding your customers' data can only protect it if the contract lets you know quickly and check. SITL-POL-013 section 6.3 lists what is essential.
T7.2-9.h1: Read the clause table in POL-013 section 6.3 and pick what protects customer data, not what helps the supplier or marketing.
T7.2-9.h3: Find the table in section 6.3. It lists clauses by supplier tier. Work out the tier of a supplier that holds customer data, then read which clauses the table marks as essential for it. Check each choice against the table, and ask whether a commercial term protects the data at all.

T8.1-1.why: At work a tabletop only teaches if everyone starts from the same facts. Missing the timeline or the data involved early skews every later decision.
T8.1-1.h1: Read the scenario and each inject in order. Which facts would change what you do first: who, what data, when?
T8.1-1.h3: Read the scenario once for context, then the injects slowly, noting times. The injects are in UTC but the office works in Manila time, so convert before comparing anything. Look for what is affected, whether personal data is involved, and the moment the organisation first knew. Pick facts that will matter later when you set phases and deadlines, not colour or detail that does not drive a decision.

T8.1-10.why: At work staff who cannot report a suspicious e-mail leave the security team blind to early warning signs, and incidents start later than they need to.
T8.1-10.h1: Which control is about the people and the channel for raising something suspicious, as opposed to handling it afterwards?
T8.1-10.h3: Separate three jobs: planning for incidents, deciding what is an incident, and the act of staff raising a concern. The scenario's problem is that people did not know how to raise it. Ask which control covers a simple, known way to report events, and ignore the ones about what the response team does once it has been told. Compare each option's wording against that single gap.

T8.1-11.why: At work, evidence with an inconsistent name or no timestamp cannot be found or trusted later. The receipt is what proves the file was fixed at a point in time.
T8.1-11.h1: Are your file names built from the same parts, in the same order, as the convention? Did the receipt appear?
T8.1-11.h3: List each part the convention names (office or programme code, task, document code, version, extension) and build each name from them, one for each of the tabletop record and the tracker. Compare two names side by side; they should differ only in the document code. Save, then read the receipt: a hash and a UTC time must both be there. Only after that mark the step complete; if the receipt lacks either, the save did not finish.

T8.1-2.why: At work a team that cannot say which stage an event belongs to will skip stages, for instance containing before preserving evidence or closing without a lessons review.
T8.1-2.h1: For each inject, ask what the team is doing at that moment: getting ready, judging, acting, learning or securing evidence?
T8.1-2.h3: Read the policy's life-cycle section so you know what each stage covers. Then take each inject and ask what its main verb is: a plan or training already in place, someone judging severity, someone containing, someone gathering or sealing artefacts, someone reviewing afterwards. Two injects can look alike; choose by what the team is doing, not by the incident's topic. Check the injects are in time order, so stages should flow roughly forward.

T8.1-3.why: At work the first reflex, wiping the machine, destroys the evidence needed for investigation, legal action or insurance, and that cannot be undone.
T8.1-3.h1: What does the policy's first hour say about evidence, and what does reimaging make impossible later?
T8.1-3.h3: Weigh two things: the speed of getting the device back and the value of what is on it. Ask whether anything lost by reimaging could be needed to prove what happened, who is responsible, or whether personal data left. Then read the first-hour checklist and the evidence line of the severity section and see which order they set. Test each choice against that order: what does it do first, and what record does it leave?

T8.1-4.why: At work a breach clock that starts at the wrong moment, or in the wrong time zone, means a late notification to the regulator and possible penalties.
T8.1-4.h1: Which law applies to these people, who must be told, and when did the clock actually start? Which time zone are the deadlines in?
T8.1-4.h3: First identify the jurisdiction from where the affected people are. Then find who must be notified and the time limit in the office addendum's Section 2, rule R30 and the notification procedure. Three moments compete for the start of the clock: the alert, the moment the incident was logged, and the confirmation of what the file held. The procedure's own definition of discovery time picks one. The injects are already in UTC, so add the limit to that time as it stands; converting to Manila time and back only invites a slip. Check that the date rolls over correctly.

T8.1-5.why: At work a control tracker is only useful if you have read each control's own requirements first; otherwise statuses are guessed from the control title and the audit finds the guess.
T8.1-5.h1: Before you fill any cell, ask what each of the seven controls actually requires of the office and where the SPR-08 notes will be read against that.
T8.1-5.h3: Work like an implementer: open one control's task page, read its numbered requirements, and note what evidence would prove each.
